chunks: Reducing component heating on the board. The question: What can you do at the board-level to reduce heating of a component/IC?
To keep a component cool, make less heat first. Then give the heat an easy path out of the package, spread it over copper, and finally get it into the air.
On a board, that means solid copper under the chip's exposed pad, an array of thermal vias to other layers, as much copper area as you can, and good spacing from neighbors.
Layout can matter as much as a heat sink.
Think of heat as water leaving a bathtub. The bathtub is the chip. The first fix is to turn down the tap, which means dissipating less power.
Then you widen the drain, which is the exposed pad and thermal vias. Then you add more pipes to carry it away, which is the copper planes. The sewer at the end is the air.
If the sewer is small, the tub still fills up.
The exposed pad is soldered to top copper; the via array moves heat down through the poorly conducting FR-4 into the inner plane and the bottom copper, and each copper layer spreads it sideways.
The vias are only useful if they land on large copper.
theta JA : junction-to-ambient thermal resistance in K/W. It depends on the board. Junction temperature: T j equals T a plus P theta JA .
Exposed (thermal) pad: a metal pad under a package that carries die heat to the board.
Thermal via: a plated hole under that pad that moves heat to other layers ("Via stitching and when to use it").
Thermal spreading: heat flowing sideways through a copper plane or pour ("Power planes and shapes vs traces").
A linear regulator drops 5 volts to 3. 3 volts at 0. 5 amps. It dissipates (5 minus 3. 3) times 0. 5 equals 0. 85 watts. With theta JA equals 60 K/W, the junction rises 0.
85 times 60 equals 51 degrees Celsius above ambient. A buck converter at 90 percent efficiency dissipates only 3. 3 times 0. 5 times (1 over 0. 9 minus 1) about 0.
18 watts, which is about 11 degrees Celsius of rise. That is the whole idea.
"First dissipate less, for example a buck instead of an LDO.

Then give heat a path: solder the exposed pad to a big top-layer copper area with a solid connection and an array of thermal vias into inner planes and the bottom side, use as much copper as possible, and heavier copper if needed.
Spread hot parts apart, keep them near airflow and away from sensitive parts, and finally check with a thermal camera. If the board can't do it, add a heat sink."
